name: Academic Writing
description: An elective course developing essential academic writing skills including thesis construction, evidence integration, citation, and discipline-specific writing for college preparation.

modules.title: What is Academic Writing
modules.objectives: Define academic writing and distinguish it from other writing modes; identify the key characteristics of effective academic prose.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 1.3 — compare audience, purpose, genre and evidence across texts.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 1 — What is Academic Writing lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL rhetorical situation — compare author, audience, purpose and setting in the three sample texts.
modules.assignment: Compare three short, fictional texts about a school library staying open later: (A) social post: 'Please keep the library open after 6! I need a quiet place to study.' (B) news brief: 'The school is considering a later library closing time; staff will review usage and staffing.' (C) academic-style claim: 'A decision about library hours should compare documented student use with staffing capacity.' Write 250–350 words naming each text's audience and purpose, then compare register, claim, evidence (including what evidence is missing), and structure. Submit one document with the three labeled comparisons and a revised academic-style paragraph of 100–150 words; label any hypothetical details as hypothetical. Evaluation: accurate genre/audience analysis (30%), evidence/claim distinction (30%), justified revision (30%), clear attribution and organization (10%).

modules.title: Reading Academic Texts
modules.objectives: Apply active reading strategies to academic texts including annotation, identifying thesis and evidence, and engaging with complex arguments. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 1.5 — annotate, summarize, paraphrase and question a text while reading.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 2 — Reading Academic Texts lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax 16.5 — identify a claim, supporting passages and an interpretive question in a short text.
modules.assignment: Read the OpenStax 1.5 section linked in this module, especially 'Responding to Understand: Summary' and 'Responding to Clarify: Paraphrase.' Annotate one 250–400 word passage from that page: label its central claim, two supporting details, one unfamiliar term, and one question for the author. Submit a link to the passage, an annotated screenshot or typed annotation table keyed to short quoted phrases, and a 180–220 word response that summarizes the claim before explaining your question. Evaluation: accurate claim and evidence (35%), useful annotations/question (35%), fair summary with source citation (20%), readable organization (10%). Do not copy the whole passage into the submission.

modules.title: Critical Thinking
modules.objectives: Apply critical thinking skills to evaluate arguments, identify assumptions, assess evidence quality, and develop independent analytical reasoning. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 11.1 — evaluate reasoning strategies and distinguish stronger evidence from an appealing claim.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 3 — Critical Thinking lesson video.
modules.video2Note: Crash Course Philosophy #2 — How to Argue (optional reasoning supplement).
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL Toulmin method — label claim, grounds, warrant and counterclaim in the two practice arguments.
modules.assignment: Compare two fictional school-library arguments. A: 'The school should pilot later library hours one day each week because after-school students may need quiet space; usage counts would show whether a longer schedule helps.' B: 'The school should keep current hours until it measures staffing capacity and current use; longer hours may divert support from the daytime program.' Neither passage supplies actual usage or staffing data. In 350–450 words, identify each claim and one assumption, compare the evidence offered and what is missing, explain which proposed decision is better supported by the present information, and name two facts that could change your judgment. Submit a two-column comparison table plus the paragraph. Evaluation: fair representation of both positions (25%), explicit assumptions (25%), evidence-quality reasoning and uncertainty (35%), clear organization (15%). Treat both passages as hypothetical; no personal disclosure or outside source is required.

modules.title: Thesis & Argument
modules.objectives: Construct a strong, specific, and debatable thesis statement; understand the relationship between thesis, topic sentences, and supporting evidence. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 10.3 — distinguish a debatable thesis from its supporting reasons and evidence.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 4 — Thesis & Argument lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax 10.5 — draft and revise a focused thesis, then outline reasons and evidence.
modules.assignment: Draft one thesis on each of these five practice topics: library hours, school start time, classroom phone rules, campus recycling, and public transit access. For each, mark whether it is specific, debatable and supportable with evidence; revise any thesis that fails a criterion. Select the strongest revised thesis and add an outline with two reasons, the kind of evidence needed for each reason, and one plausible counterargument. Submit the five before/after thesis pairs and the outline. Evaluation: specificity and debatable claims (35%), justified revisions (30%), reasons/evidence/counterargument alignment (25%), clarity (10%). These are practice positions; no particular policy stance is required.

modules.title: Body Paragraph Structure
modules.objectives: Construct body paragraphs with clear topic sentences, integrated evidence, and analytical commentary using the PEEL or similar framework. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 8.5 — organize body paragraphs by point, evidence and analysis.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 5 — Body Paragraph Structure lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL On Paragraphs — use unity, topic sentence, coherence and development as a revision checklist.
modules.assignment: Use your revised Module 4 thesis, or this practice thesis: 'A school library should test one later opening day each week before extending all weekday hours.' Draft three body paragraphs that each develop a different reason. In each paragraph, mark the topic sentence, one cited piece of verifiable evidence or a clearly labeled hypothetical example, two sentences explaining how that support bears on the reason, and a link back to the thesis. Submit the paragraphs plus a four-column point/evidence/explanation/link checklist for each. Evaluation: distinct thesis-linked points (25%), credible or honestly labeled support (25%), analysis rather than summary (35%), coherent paragraph flow and citation (15%).

modules.title: Evidence & Quotation
modules.objectives: Select and integrate quotations and paraphrases effectively; apply the quotation sandwich method to analyze evidence rather than letting it speak for itself.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 12.6 — introduce a quotation, preserve wording and explain its relevance.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 6 — Evidence & Quotation lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL — decide when to quote, paraphrase or summarize a passage and retain source attribution.
modules.assignment: Read OpenStax Writing Guide 12.6 linked in this module. Choose three short passages from that section (one or two sentences each) that illustrate source integration. For each, submit the original passage location, a narrowly selected quotation with a signal phrase and citation, and two original sentences explaining how the quotation supports a claim you state. Revise one weak quotation introduction and explain why the revision is clearer. Submit a document with three labeled quotation sandwiches and the revision note. Evaluation: accurate quotation/citation (30%), purposeful signal phrase (20%), analysis tied to claim (40%), concise organization (10%). Do not reproduce long source passages.

modules.title: Paraphrase & Summary
modules.objectives: Accurately paraphrase and summarize source material while maintaining the original meaning; distinguish between acceptable paraphrase and plagiarism. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 13.5 — keep exact quotes, paraphrases, summaries and source notes distinct.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 7 — Paraphrase & Summary lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL paraphrasing exercise — restate a short passage accurately and add its source citation.
modules.assignment: Select three short passages (one or two sentences each) from the linked OpenStax 13.5 section. For each, give a link or heading and a brief original excerpt, then write (a) a faithful paraphrase in a new sentence structure, (b) a one-sentence summary that keeps only the central idea, and (c) an in-text source citation. Add a two-sentence explanation of why your paraphrase is more than synonym substitution. Submit a three-row comparison table and the explanation. Evaluation: preserved meaning (30%), genuinely new wording/structure (25%), summary versus paraphrase distinction (20%), traceable citations (15%), explanation (10%).

modules.title: Citation Styles (MLA/APA)
modules.objectives: Format citations and reference lists in both MLA and APA style; understand when each style is used and the principles behind documentation. Students will analyze examples, explain the relevant concept in context, and create a short written or visual product that demonstrates mastery.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Writing Guide 14.2 — compare the purpose and basic structure of MLA and APA documentation.
modules.videoNote: GIIS Academic Writing Module 8 — Citation Styles (MLA/APA) lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Purdue OWL APA 7 overview — verify author-date citations and references; compare with MLA examples in the OpenStax reading.
modules.assignment: Use three real, public course sources: the linked OpenStax 14.2 page, Purdue OWL's APA 7 guide (https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/apa_style/apa_formatting_and_style_guide/index.html), and Purdue OWL's MLA 9 guide (https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/research_and_citation/mla_style/mla_formatting_and_style_guide/index.html). Record each page's visible author/organization, title, date (or n.d. if absent), and URL; do not invent missing metadata. Make an MLA Works Cited entry and an APA References entry for each source, plus one in-text citation in each style for a paraphrase of one source. Submit a six-entry citation table and 120–160 words comparing author/date placement, title/format and in-text conventions. Evaluation: source metadata accuracy (25%), MLA form (25%), APA form (25%), meaningful comparison and clear writing (25%).

quizQuestions.question: Which characteristic best distinguishes academic writing from personal writing?
options: Academic writing is always longer.
Academic writing uses formal language, evidence-based reasoning, and precise, objective claims.
Academic writing avoids using any sources.
Academic writing is only written in third person.
quizQuestions.answer: Academic writing uses formal language, evidence-based reasoning, and precise, objective claims.
quizQuestions.explanation: Academic writing is characterized by formal register, evidence-based argument, precision, objectivity, and proper citation—unlike personal writing, which is more subjective.

quizQuestions.question: Academic writing is considered 'formal' because it:
options: Uses contractions freely
Avoids slang, contractions, and casual expressions in favor of precise, professional language
Always discusses formal events
Requires exactly five paragraphs
quizQuestions.answer: Avoids slang, contractions, and casual expressions in favor of precise, professional language
quizQuestions.explanation: Formal academic writing avoids contractions (use 'do not' not 'don't'), slang, and colloquial expressions, using precise professional vocabulary instead.

quizQuestions.question: A writer is turning a personal note about later library hours into a short academic argument. Which revision best fits readers who expect a checkable claim?
options: I just know later hours would be amazing for everyone.
The library should test one later opening day and compare usage with staffing costs before expanding hours.
People who disagree with later hours do not care about students.
The library is a building that currently has opening hours.
quizQuestions.answer: The library should test one later opening day and compare usage with staffing costs before expanding hours.
quizQuestions.explanation: The revision gives a specific, testable position and names evidence needed for an academic audience rather than relying on enthusiasm or an unsupported judgment.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: The intended audience for most academic writing is...
quizQuestions.answer: The intended audience for most academic writing is an educated academic or professional reader who expects clear reasoning, formal language, credible evidence, and precise claims.
quizQuestions.explanation: This answer is stronger because it names both the audience and the expectations that shape academic style: evidence, precision, organization, and an objective tone.

quizQuestions.question: Annotation in active reading means:
options: Reading quickly without stopping to make notes
Writing notes, questions, and observations in the margins of a text as you read
Copying out important sentences verbatim
Summarizing the text after finishing it
quizQuestions.answer: Writing notes, questions, and observations in the margins of a text as you read
quizQuestions.explanation: Annotation is active engagement with the text—marking key ideas, asking questions, identifying the thesis and evidence—as you read rather than passively processing.

quizQuestions.question: When reading an academic text, identifying the thesis is important because:
options: The thesis tells you the length of the paper
The thesis states the central argument that organizes and motivates the entire text
The thesis always appears in the conclusion
The thesis is the least important part of an academic text
quizQuestions.answer: The thesis states the central argument that organizes and motivates the entire text
quizQuestions.explanation: The thesis is the central claim of an academic text; identifying it allows you to understand how all other parts of the text relate to and support that central argument.

quizQuestions.question: A reading response is most useful when it:
options: Simply summarizes what you read without personal engagement
Identifies the author's argument and engages critically with questions it raises for you
Agrees with everything the author argues
Is as short as possible
quizQuestions.answer: Identifies the author's argument and engages critically with questions it raises for you
quizQuestions.explanation: A reading response demonstrates active engagement—identifying the argument, asking critical questions, and connecting ideas to your own understanding.

quizQuestions.question: A passage claims that later library hours would improve access but gives no usage figures. Which margin note best shows active reading?
options: Nice sentence.
What usage data and staffing limits would test this access claim?
Copy this sentence into my response without attribution.
Ignore the missing data because the claim sounds reasonable.
quizQuestions.answer: What usage data and staffing limits would test this access claim?
quizQuestions.explanation: An active reader marks the claim and asks for evidence that could confirm or limit it.

quizQuestions.question: Critical thinking in academic writing requires the ability to:
options: Accept all published arguments without questioning them
Evaluate the validity of arguments, assess evidence quality, and identify assumptions
Memorize all facts presented in sources
Use the most technical vocabulary possible
quizQuestions.answer: Evaluate the validity of arguments, assess evidence quality, and identify assumptions
quizQuestions.explanation: Critical thinking involves actively questioning and evaluating—not simply accepting—arguments, evidence, and assumptions presented in academic texts.

quizQuestions.question: In argument analysis, an assumption is:
options: A piece of evidence that is explicitly stated
An unstated belief or premise that the argument takes for granted without proving
The thesis statement of the argument
A direct quotation from a source
quizQuestions.answer: An unstated belief or premise that the argument takes for granted without proving
quizQuestions.explanation: Assumptions are unstated premises—beliefs the arguer takes for granted and does not explicitly justify, which may or may not be valid.

quizQuestions.question: Evaluating evidence quality requires asking:
options: Only how recent the evidence is
Whether the evidence is credible, relevant to the claim, and sufficient to support the conclusion
Whether the evidence appears impressive
Only whether the evidence is from a primary source
quizQuestions.answer: Whether the evidence is credible, relevant to the claim, and sufficient to support the conclusion
quizQuestions.explanation: Quality evidence evaluation checks credibility (is the source reliable?), relevance (does it directly support the claim?), and sufficiency (is there enough evidence?).

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: A well-supported academic claim is one that...
quizQuestions.answer: A well-supported academic claim is specific, debatable, and backed by credible, relevant, and sufficient evidence rather than opinion alone.
quizQuestions.explanation: The key distinction is support. Academic claims need evidence that actually connects to the claim and gives readers enough reason to accept the argument.

quizQuestions.question: A thesis statement is 'debatable' when:
options: Everyone agrees with it as an obvious fact
Reasonable people could argue the opposite position and it requires evidence to support
It contains many complex academic words
It is stated in the first sentence of the essay
quizQuestions.answer: Reasonable people could argue the opposite position and it requires evidence to support
quizQuestions.explanation: A debatable thesis takes a position that reasonable people could disagree with, requiring evidence and argument to support rather than being self-evidently true.

quizQuestions.question: Which is the strongest thesis statement?
options: Social media exists and people use it a lot.
This essay will discuss the effects of social media.
Social media is bad for teenagers.
Excessive social media use correlates with increased anxiety in adolescents by limiting face-to-face interaction and creating unrealistic social comparisons.
quizQuestions.answer: Excessive social media use correlates with increased anxiety in adolescents by limiting face-to-face interaction and creating unrealistic social comparisons.
quizQuestions.explanation: The strongest thesis is specific, debatable, and identifies the 'how' and 'why'—it previews the evidence and reasoning that will follow.

quizQuestions.question: Topic sentences in body paragraphs should:
options: Introduce a completely new topic unrelated to the thesis
State the main point of the paragraph and connect it clearly to the thesis
Be a quotation from a source
Always start with 'Furthermore'
quizQuestions.answer: State the main point of the paragraph and connect it clearly to the thesis
quizQuestions.explanation: A topic sentence states the paragraph's main point and connects it to the thesis, creating coherence between body paragraphs and the central argument.

quizQuestions.question: A thesis that says 'There are pros and cons to social media' is weak because:
options: It is too long
It is too specific and narrow
It fails to take a position—it simply acknowledges that different views exist
It contains informal language
quizQuestions.answer: It fails to take a position—it simply acknowledges that different views exist
quizQuestions.explanation: A 'pros and cons' thesis avoids taking a debatable position; a strong thesis makes a specific claim that the essay will argue and prove.

quizQuestions.question: In a PEEL paragraph, what does the 'L' (Link) accomplish?
options: Lists additional evidence
Connects the paragraph's point back to the thesis and transitions to the next paragraph
Lists all sources used in the paragraph
Introduces a counterargument
quizQuestions.answer: Connects the paragraph's point back to the thesis and transitions to the next paragraph
quizQuestions.explanation: The Link (L) in PEEL closes the paragraph by tying the point back to the thesis and providing a smooth transition, maintaining essay coherence.

quizQuestions.question: Analysis in a body paragraph should explain:
options: What the source says, without any original interpretation
How and why the evidence supports the paragraph's claim and ultimately the thesis
A summary of all sources on the topic
The biography of the author being cited
quizQuestions.answer: How and why the evidence supports the paragraph's claim and ultimately the thesis
quizQuestions.explanation: Analysis is the writer's original interpretation—explaining the significance of the evidence and the logical connection between the evidence and the claim.

quizQuestions.question: A paragraph begins, 'A later library closing time could help students with after-school activities.' Which next move best develops that point?
options: Start an unrelated point about cafeteria menus.
Give a relevant usage or schedule example, cite its source if factual, and explain how it bears on access.
Repeat the same topic sentence in different words three times.
End the paragraph before offering any support.
quizQuestions.answer: Give a relevant usage or schedule example, cite its source if factual, and explain how it bears on access.
quizQuestions.explanation: The paragraph needs support and analysis tied to its single topic; repetition or unrelated material does not develop the claim.

quizQuestions.question: A draft says, 'Twenty students used the library after 5 p.m. This proves later hours are always better.' Which revision adds responsible analysis?
options: The count suggests some demand on that day, but the writer needs more dates and staffing information before recommending a permanent schedule.
Twenty is a number, so the claim is fully proven.
Delete the count and keep the conclusion.
Change 'twenty' to 'many' without checking the source.
quizQuestions.answer: The count suggests some demand on that day, but the writer needs more dates and staffing information before recommending a permanent schedule.
quizQuestions.explanation: The revision interprets the evidence, states its limit, and connects the support to a proportionate claim.

quizQuestions.question: The 'quotation sandwich' method requires:
options: Using only bread-shaped formatting in your essay
Introducing a quotation, providing it, and then analyzing it—never letting a quotation stand alone
Using exactly three quotations per paragraph
Placing all quotations at the beginning of paragraphs
quizQuestions.answer: Introducing a quotation, providing it, and then analyzing it—never letting a quotation stand alone
quizQuestions.explanation: The quotation sandwich: context/signal phrase + quotation + analysis. No quotation should appear without both an introduction and follow-up analysis.

quizQuestions.question: A signal phrase in academic writing serves to:
options: Replace the need for a citation
Introduce a quotation or paraphrase by naming the author and providing context
Signal the end of the essay
Indicate that a new paragraph is beginning
quizQuestions.answer: Introduce a quotation or paraphrase by naming the author and providing context
quizQuestions.explanation: Signal phrases attribute borrowed material to its source and provide context before the quotation or paraphrase, smoothly integrating evidence into the argument.

quizQuestions.question: Selecting the best quotation for a body paragraph means choosing:
options: The longest quotation available
A specific passage that provides the most precise, relevant evidence for the paragraph's claim
Any quotation from the source, regardless of relevance
The most difficult to understand passage
quizQuestions.answer: A specific passage that provides the most precise, relevant evidence for the paragraph's claim
quizQuestions.explanation: Effective quotation selection requires finding the specific passage that provides the most direct, relevant support for the paragraph's particular analytical claim.

quizQuestions.question: A student drops a quotation into a paragraph with no introduction or explanation. Which revision best integrates it?
options: Add a signal phrase naming the source, keep an accurate citation, and explain how the quoted words support the paragraph's claim.
Use a longer quotation so no explanation is necessary.
Remove quotation marks while keeping the exact wording.
Move the quotation to the first line and leave it unexplained.
quizQuestions.answer: Add a signal phrase naming the source, keep an accurate citation, and explain how the quoted words support the paragraph's claim.
quizQuestions.explanation: Readers need to know who supplied the words and why the selected passage matters to the writer's claim.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: When should a writer choose to paraphrase rather than quote directly?
quizQuestions.answer: A writer should paraphrase when the source's idea matters more than its exact wording and the writer can restate that idea accurately in their own words while still citing the source.
quizQuestions.explanation: Paraphrasing helps integrate evidence smoothly into the writer's argument, but it still requires accuracy, original wording and structure, and proper citation.

quizQuestions.question: Proper paraphrasing requires:
options: Changing only a few words in the original sentence
Completely restating the idea in your own words and sentence structure, then citing the source
Copying the source verbatim and changing the font
Using the original sentence structure but different vocabulary
quizQuestions.answer: Completely restating the idea in your own words and sentence structure, then citing the source
quizQuestions.explanation: True paraphrase requires completely restating the idea in your own words and sentence structure—just changing a few words while keeping the original structure is patchwriting (a form of plagiarism).

quizQuestions.question: Patchwriting is a form of academic dishonesty because:
options: It uses too many sources
It makes minimal changes to the original text, creating an inaccurate appearance of original expression
It cites too many authors
It uses the wrong citation format
quizQuestions.answer: It makes minimal changes to the original text, creating an inaccurate appearance of original expression
quizQuestions.explanation: Patchwriting (swapping a few words while keeping the original structure) falsely presents near-copied work as original paraphrase, which is a form of plagiarism.

quizQuestions.question: A hypothetical source says, 'Extending library hours gave more students a quiet place after school.' Which draft is a genuine paraphrase that still needs a citation?
options: After school, more students could study quietly because the library stayed open longer (source citation).
Extending library hours gave more students a quiet place after school, with no quotation marks or citation.
Extending library hours provided more students a quiet place after school (source citation).
Libraries are good.
quizQuestions.answer: After school, more students could study quietly because the library stayed open longer (source citation).
quizQuestions.explanation: The first option preserves the idea while restructuring the sentence and attributing the source; the third mostly substitutes synonyms in the original syntax.

quizQuestions.question: Short response: Complete this statement: A successful paraphrase test is...
quizQuestions.answer: A successful paraphrase test is whether the new sentence preserves the original meaning while using the writer's own wording and sentence structure and giving credit to the source.
quizQuestions.explanation: Changing only a few words is patchwriting. A real paraphrase shows understanding by restating the idea independently and citing the source.

quizQuestions.question: APA citation style is most commonly used in:
options: Literature, languages, and cultural studies
Social sciences, education, and psychology
Medical and clinical research
Legal studies and law reviews
quizQuestions.answer: Social sciences, education, and psychology
quizQuestions.explanation: APA (American Psychological Association) style is the standard in social sciences, education, and psychology, emphasizing publication dates.

quizQuestions.question: MLA in-text citations for a direct quote from author Smith on page 45 appear as:
options: (Smith 45)
[Smith 45]
(45, Smith)
quizQuestions.answer: (Smith 45)
quizQuestions.explanation: MLA format: (Author's last name page number) with no comma and no 'p.' — (Smith 45).

quizQuestions.question: APA in-text citations include which elements?
options: Author's full name, title, and URL
Author's last name, year of publication, and page/paragraph number for direct quotes
Author's first name and publisher
Journal title and volume number
quizQuestions.answer: Author's last name, year of publication, and page/paragraph number for direct quotes
quizQuestions.explanation: APA in-text: (Author, Year, p. #) — e.g., (Smith, 2020, p. 45) for direct quotations; (Smith, 2020) for paraphrase.

quizQuestions.question: Which pair correctly names the end-of-paper source list in MLA and APA 7 style?
options: MLA: Works Cited; APA: References
MLA: References; APA: Works Cited
MLA: Abstract; APA: Bibliography
MLA: Footnotes; APA: Appendix
quizQuestions.answer: MLA: Works Cited; APA: References
quizQuestions.explanation: MLA normally labels the source list Works Cited; APA 7 labels it References. Both lists identify works actually used and follow their assigned formatting rules.

questions.question: Which characteristic best defines academic writing?
options: Uses casual, conversational language
Formal register, evidence-based argument, and precise claims with proper citation
Always written in first person
Avoids using any outside sources
questions.answer: Formal register, evidence-based argument, and precise claims with proper citation
questions.explanation: Academic writing is characterized by formal language, claims supported by credible evidence, and proper citation of all sources.

questions.question: Active reading of an academic text involves:
options: Reading as quickly as possible
Annotating, identifying the thesis, and engaging critically with arguments
Reading only the abstract and conclusion
Copying important sentences verbatim
questions.answer: Annotating, identifying the thesis, and engaging critically with arguments
questions.explanation: Active reading involves annotation, identifying the thesis and evidence, and critically engaging with the author's argument—not passive processing.

questions.question: An assumption in an argument is:
options: A stated piece of evidence
An unstated belief the argument takes for granted
The thesis statement
A direct quotation
questions.answer: An unstated belief the argument takes for granted
questions.explanation: An assumption is an unstated premise the argument depends on without explicit proof.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Which thesis statement is the most specific and debatable?
options: A focused thesis that takes a clear position and can be supported with evidence
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
A sentence that changes only a few source words
questions.answer: A focused thesis that takes a clear position and can be supported with evidence
questions.explanation: The best answer is "A focused thesis that takes a clear position and can be supported with evidence" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: In a PEEL paragraph, analysis (E—Explain) should:
options: Restate what the quotation says in different words
Explain how and why the evidence connects to and proves the paragraph's claim
Provide additional quotations
Introduce the next paragraph's topic
questions.answer: Explain how and why the evidence connects to and proves the paragraph's claim
questions.explanation: The Explain element is the writer's original interpretation—showing the logical connection between the evidence and the claim being made.

questions.question: A signal phrase does which of the following?
options: Indicates the end of the essay
Introduces borrowed material by naming the author and providing context
Replaces the need for an in-text citation
Lists sources alphabetically
questions.answer: Introduces borrowed material by naming the author and providing context
questions.explanation: A signal phrase smoothly introduces quoted or paraphrased material, attributing it to its source before the citation.

questions.question: True paraphrasing requires the writer to:
questions.answer: True paraphrasing requires the writer to restate the source idea accurately in their own words and sentence structure while still citing the original source.
questions.explanation: The answer should distinguish real paraphrase from patchwriting: the meaning is preserved, but the wording and structure are genuinely the student's own.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: MLA format in-text citations include:
options: The author's last name and page number when available
Author, year, and page number
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
questions.answer: The author's last name and page number when available
questions.explanation: The best answer is "The author's last name and page number when available" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: Boolean operator AND in a database search:
options: Broadens results to include either term
Narrows results by requiring both terms to appear
Excludes one term from all results
Searches for exact phrase sequences
questions.answer: Narrows results by requiring both terms to appear
questions.explanation: AND narrows searches—both search terms must appear in results, reducing quantity but increasing relevance.

questions.question: A literature review is organized most effectively by:
options: Summarizing each source separately in alphabetical order
Themes, debates, or methodological approaches in the research
The order in which sources were found
Publication date from oldest to newest
questions.answer: Themes, debates, or methodological approaches in the research
questions.explanation: Thematic organization synthesizes sources by shared ideas, creating an analytical map of the field rather than isolated summaries.

questions.question: In Academic Writing midterm concepts, An abstract is written:
options: Before the paper to plan its structure
After the paper is complete, summarizing its finished content
By a classmate who reads the draft
As a replacement for the introduction
questions.answer: After the paper is complete, summarizing its finished content
questions.explanation: The abstract summarizes the completed paper—it can only be written accurately after the paper is finished.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Patchwriting is a form of plagiarism because it:
options: It keeps the source structure or ideas while changing only some words without proper attribution
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
A sentence that changes only a few source words
questions.answer: It keeps the source structure or ideas while changing only some words without proper attribution
questions.explanation: The best answer is "It keeps the source structure or ideas while changing only some words without proper attribution" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: Humanities writing differs from social science writing primarily in its:
options: Use of longer papers
Emphasis on textual interpretation and close reading rather than empirical data and statistical methods
Avoidance of all citations
Use of APA citation format
questions.answer: Emphasis on textual interpretation and close reading rather than empirical data and statistical methods
questions.explanation: Humanities writing centers on interpretation and textual analysis; social science writing emphasizes empirical evidence, data, and theoretical frameworks.

questions.question: Self-plagiarism occurs when a student:
questions.answer: Self-plagiarism occurs when a student reuses their own earlier work for a new assignment without permission, disclosure, or appropriate citation.
questions.explanation: Even though the work is the student's, submitting it again can misrepresent the amount of new learning or effort unless the instructor allows it.

questions.question: A 'gap' in the research literature refers to:
options: A source you could not access
An aspect of the topic not yet adequately addressed by existing research
A discrepancy between two sources
A source published before 2000
questions.answer: An aspect of the topic not yet adequately addressed by existing research
questions.explanation: A research gap is an underexplored aspect of a topic that existing literature has not adequately addressed, justifying new research.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: IMRaD structure in natural science writing stands for:
options: Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion
Introduction, Main argument, References, and Discussion
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
questions.answer: Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion
questions.explanation: The best answer is "Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: A hanging indent format means that:
options: Every line of the citation is indented equally
The first line is flush left and all subsequent lines are indented
Only the author's name appears on the first line
The last line of each citation is indented
questions.answer: The first line is flush left and all subsequent lines are indented
questions.explanation: Hanging indent: first line flush left, all continuation lines indented—used in both MLA Works Cited and APA References.

questions.question: The significance section of an abstract explains:
options: The author's academic background
Why the research findings matter and their implications
The budget for the research project
The limitations of the study only
questions.answer: Why the research findings matter and their implications
questions.explanation: The significance or implications section explains why the research matters—what it contributes to knowledge, practice, or policy in the field.

questions.question: Effective peer review requires that feedback be:
options: General and vague to avoid hurting feelings
Specific, actionable, and grounded in the text being reviewed
Only positive observations
Written as briefly as possible
questions.answer: Specific, actionable, and grounded in the text being reviewed
questions.explanation: Useful peer feedback identifies specific passages, explains what works and what needs improvement, and provides concrete revision suggestions.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: The quotation sandwich method requires that every quotation be:
options: Introduced, quoted, and then explained or analyzed in the writer's own words
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
A sentence that changes only a few source words
questions.answer: Introduced, quoted, and then explained or analyzed in the writer's own words
questions.explanation: The best answer is "Introduced, quoted, and then explained or analyzed in the writer's own words" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: Common knowledge does not require citation. Which of the following IS common knowledge?
questions.answer: Common knowledge is a widely known, easily verified fact, such as a basic historical date or scientific fact, not a specialized claim, statistic, quotation, or interpretation from a source.
questions.explanation: The important test is whether an educated reader would already know the fact or could confirm it in many standard references; source-specific information still needs citation.

questions.question: APA citation style is most commonly used in which fields?
options: Literature and the arts
Social and behavioral sciences, education, and psychology
Medical and legal studies
Philosophy and theology
questions.answer: Social and behavioral sciences, education, and psychology
questions.explanation: APA is the standard for social and behavioral sciences, education, and psychology, emphasizing the currency of research through publication dates.

questions.question: Synthesizing sources in a literature review means:
options: Summarizing each source completely and separately
Integrating sources to show relationships, agreements, and contradictions across the research
Selecting only one authoritative source to rely on
Avoiding direct comparison between sources
questions.answer: Integrating sources to show relationships, agreements, and contradictions across the research
questions.explanation: Synthesis weaves sources together—showing patterns, agreements, and debates across the literature—creating an analytical overview rather than a series of summaries.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Adapting academic writing to a specific discipline requires understanding:
options: The discipline's questions, evidence standards, audience, conventions, and citation practices
Only which citation format to use
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
questions.answer: The discipline's questions, evidence standards, audience, conventions, and citation practices
questions.explanation: The best answer is "The discipline's questions, evidence standards, audience, conventions, and citation practices" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: The best defense against accidental plagiarism is:
options: Only using your own ideas with no research
Careful note-taking that distinguishes your ideas from sources, combined with citation of all borrowed material
Using a thesaurus to change every word in a paraphrase
Avoiding all direct quotations
questions.answer: Careful note-taking that distinguishes your ideas from sources, combined with citation of all borrowed material
questions.explanation: Organized research notes that clearly separate your ideas from source material, combined with careful citation practice, prevent accidental plagiarism.

questions.question: A research question should be refined during the research process when:
options: It is always inappropriate to change the original question
Initial investigation reveals the question is too broad, too narrow, or that the literature addresses a more specific angle
The instructor assigns a new topic
You run out of sources
questions.answer: Initial investigation reveals the question is too broad, too narrow, or that the literature addresses a more specific angle
questions.explanation: Research questions naturally evolve as researchers learn more about a topic—refinement in response to evidence is a sign of intellectual engagement.

questions.question: A topic sentence must be directly connected to the thesis because:
options: They should be the same sentence repeated
Each body paragraph must develop one aspect of the thesis—disconnected paragraphs undermine essay coherence
Topic sentences should introduce new topics unrelated to the thesis
It makes the paper appear longer
questions.answer: Each body paragraph must develop one aspect of the thesis—disconnected paragraphs undermine essay coherence
questions.explanation: Essay coherence requires that every body paragraph's topic sentence directly develops the thesis—unrelated paragraphs fragment the argument.

questions.question: Brackets [ ] in a direct quotation indicate that the writer has:
questions.answer: Brackets in a direct quotation indicate that the writer has inserted, clarified, or slightly changed words inside the quotation while preserving the original meaning.
questions.explanation: Brackets make the writer's additions transparent, such as clarifying a pronoun or adjusting grammar so the quotation fits the sentence.

questions.question: An effective research note system distinguishes:
options: Sources by their color-coded covers
Your own ideas and analysis from paraphrased source material and direct quotations
Only between primary and secondary sources
Sources by their length only
questions.answer: Your own ideas and analysis from paraphrased source material and direct quotations
questions.explanation: Effective research notes clearly separate the researcher's own ideas from paraphrased material and direct quotations—preventing accidental plagiarism during writing.

questions.question: Global revision addresses which type of issues?
options: Spelling and punctuation errors
Thesis clarity, argument structure, evidence integration, and paragraph development
Font and formatting choices
Page numbering and margins
questions.answer: Thesis clarity, argument structure, evidence integration, and paragraph development
questions.explanation: Global revision addresses big-picture issues that affect the essay's intellectual effectiveness—thesis, structure, argument, evidence—not surface-level mechanics.

questions.question: Why must a paraphrase always be cited even though it uses the writer's own words?
options: It does not need to be cited—paraphrase is free from attribution requirements
Because the idea belongs to the original author, even when expressed in different words
Only paraphrases longer than two sentences need citation
Only APA requires citation of paraphrases, not MLA
questions.answer: Because the idea belongs to the original author, even when expressed in different words
questions.explanation: Attribution is required for ideas, not just words—a paraphrase borrows the original author's intellectual contribution and must always be cited.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: The most important element of an academic thesis is that it:
options: Makes a specific, debatable claim that can be supported with evidence
Appears in the first sentence of the essay
A claim based only on personal preference
A summary that gives no evidence or citation
questions.answer: Makes a specific, debatable claim that can be supported with evidence
questions.explanation: The best answer is "Makes a specific, debatable claim that can be supported with evidence" because it directly addresses the concept being assessed.

questions.question: Social science writing typically uses which type of evidence?
options: Close textual analysis of literary works
Empirical data, research studies, and statistical analysis
Historical primary documents only
Personal anecdotes and individual experience
questions.answer: Empirical data, research studies, and statistical analysis
questions.explanation: Social sciences rely on empirical evidence—data from studies, surveys, experiments—organized within theoretical frameworks from the discipline.

questions.question: Academic integrity requires that students:
options: Use only their own ideas without any outside research
Credit all sources, submit original work, and represent their knowledge honestly
Always write without consulting notes during exams
Submit identical work independently for group assignments
questions.answer: Credit all sources, submit original work, and represent their knowledge honestly
questions.explanation: Academic integrity encompasses proper citation of all sources, submission of original work, and honest representation of one's own knowledge and effort.

questions.question: Writing three pieces on the same topic for different disciplines demonstrates understanding of:
questions.answer: Writing on the same topic for different disciplines demonstrates rhetorical awareness: adapting purpose, evidence, vocabulary, tone, and citation conventions to the audience and field.
questions.explanation: Different disciplines ask different kinds of questions, so a strong writer adjusts the argument and evidence instead of using one generic essay for every context.
